title: Policy is a process, so track the whole chain.
dek: How to follow an energy policy from its first announcement to the decisions that put it into practice.
author: Robert Shaw
takeaway: Before asking what a policy means for your business, establish where it stands. An ambition, an adopted law and a decision to apply it are different things.

sections.heading: Identify what you are reading
paragraphs: The European Commission’s energy website groups policy material by subjects such as energy security, affordability and the move to clean energy. Its implementation pages explain how measures are put into practice. Together, these provide starting points for a record of the policy you want to follow.

For each document, note who issued it, when it was published, what kind of document it is, where it applies and its reference number. Keep the original link and the version you read. A press release can alert you to a change. The underlying document is the better source for what has actually been proposed or decided.

sections.heading: Build an institutional timeline
paragraphs: Build a timeline that separates proposals, negotiations, adopted texts and decisions about implementation. The next step depends on the particular policy. Check the procedure rather than assuming that every measure follows the same route.

Give each entry a person responsible for reviewing it and a date for the next check. A deadline on a page is of little use if nobody follows it up. If the timetable is uncertain, record what is known and what still needs confirmation.

sections.heading: Connect the text to a research question
paragraphs: A subject such as the energy transition is too broad to guide a useful watchlist. Narrow the question to a technology, place, activity or stage of a project. Identify the part of the policy that could affect it, then note any interpretation that needs more evidence or specialist advice.

Keep the research separate from a decision about legal compliance. A policy tracker can find a relevant development and organise its documents. The organisation must still establish which rules apply to its own circumstances.

sections.heading: Make updates easy to compare
paragraphs: Use the same structure for each update. Record the previous position, the new evidence, what changed in the assessment and the next step to watch. Readers can then see what is different without having to read the whole history again.
Keep previous versions available internally. State when sources were checked. If a correction changes the meaning of an assessment, explain the change and why it was necessary.

watch: What is the document’s formal status?
Which institution is responsible for the next step?
Which part of the assessment still needs evidence or specialist review?

title: When the accounts do not add up.
dek: How to compare an official statement, a local report and a physical observation when they appear to disagree.
author: Robert Shaw
takeaway: A disagreement can be a useful finding. Keep each account, compare the time and activity it describes, and identify the evidence that could settle the difference.

sections.heading: Put the claims beside one another
paragraphs: Quoting both sides does not necessarily explain a disagreement. A useful brief shows what each source claims, when it was published, which period it describes and what the source was able to observe. This is the intended structure of the Venezuela event brief.

Put the accounts beside one another before drawing a conclusion. A statement of an organisation’s position and an independent observation may offer different kinds of evidence. The reader needs to understand the distinction.

sections.heading: Check whether the disagreement is real
paragraphs: First check that the accounts concern the same event. They may describe different activities, places or times. Something may have changed between observations, even if the reports were published close together.

Keep the original wording in the controlled research record where usage rights allow it. A public brief should contain a summary reviewed for permitted use, a source reference where appropriate and an explanation of what remains unresolved. It must not reproduce protected material or identify a confidential source.

sections.heading: Use physical observations for what they establish
paragraphs: A change in a physical measurement can be a useful lead without revealing its cause. Sensor coverage, the period used for comparison, maintenance and unrelated operating changes can affect the reading. Explain which possibilities the measurement leaves open.

Reporting from the area needs context too. Establish whether the person observed the event directly or heard about it, when it happened, what they could see and what needs protection. Being close to an event does not remove the need to check the account.

sections.heading: Make the next verification step explicit
paragraphs: Sometimes the evidence does not settle the disagreement. Say what observation could distinguish the accounts, who will review it and when the question will be checked again. A contradiction should not quietly become supporting evidence for a forecast.

The event brief remains an intended deliverable. Its usefulness depends on a source record that can be checked and a person responsible for reviewing the conclusion. A dashboard alone cannot provide either.

watch: Do the accounts describe the same time, place and activity?
What evidence could resolve the disagreement without exposing a source?

title: Give the question a deadline.
dek: How to turn a concern about an asset or contract into a question that can be answered and reviewed.
author: Robert Shaw
takeaway: A forecast needs a clear subject, an outcome, a deadline and an agreed way to decide what happened. If the evidence is missing, the answer can remain unresolved.

sections.heading: Start with the decision the client faces
paragraphs: Begin with the decision the research will support. A broad concern about labour conditions does not say what would count as an answer. Identify the asset, the activity and the outcome the client needs to understand.
Define any duration or scale that matters to the question. State which activities count and what evidence could establish the result. Another reader should be able to apply the same rule.

sections.heading: Write the evidence rule before the outcome
paragraphs: Agree the deadline and acceptable evidence before starting. Decide how to handle late reporting, contradictory sources, uncertain duration and missing information. The absence of a report does not establish that an event did not happen.

Keep the wording fixed once the question is registered. If its scope changes, retain the original and identify the revision or create a new question. Otherwise it becomes too easy to fit the question to an outcome already known.

sections.heading: Preserve the prior and every revision
paragraphs: The programme proposes initial estimates based on relevant history, expert input and analyst reasoning. Record the reasons for the estimate and any disagreement. A collection of articles does not, by itself, tell you how often a clearly defined event happened in the past.

Keep the time of every update, the evidence used, the rule or model version and the explanation for the change. If an analyst chooses how much weight to give evidence, describe that as a judgement to be tested. It should not be presented as a relationship already established by data.

sections.heading: Evaluate against a stated reference
paragraphs: For a question with a yes-or-no outcome, a Brier score measures the squared difference between the probability forecast and the recorded result. Lower scores mean less error under this rule. To show whether a method adds value, compare it with a stated reference forecast. A score on its own cannot establish that.

Decide in advance which forecast dates will be evaluated. A question should not count more heavily merely because it received more updates. Keep unresolved cases and unsuccessful forecasts in the record, and state which questions were included. The Venezuela programme does not yet claim a validated forecast record.

watch: Could another reviewer decide the outcome using the stated rule?
What happens when evidence is missing or contradictory?
Which forecast dates and reference forecast will be used to assess the results?

title: Venezuela, at the level of the asset.
dek: How the proposed Venezuela collection plan connects local evidence to the decisions around a particular asset.
author: Robert Shaw
takeaway: Start with the client’s question. A regional brief should connect relevant events to a named asset, show how precisely each event is located and protect its sources. Operating activity and an asset’s contractual position need separate evidence.

sections.heading: Begin with four priority states
paragraphs: The working plan identifies Zulia, Monagas, Bolívar and Anzoátegui as the first collection priorities. These are development priorities. They do not mean that correspondent agreements or full coverage are already in place.

Begin by asking which decisions depend on those places over the client’s chosen period. Research into access, a contractual change, labour disruption or operating continuity may require different sources. The question determines what needs to be collected.

sections.heading: Organise the local questions by zone
paragraphs: In Oriente, the proposed work covers Anzoátegui and Monagas. Questions concern facilities, terminals, supplies, labour, contractors and regional authorities. In Occidente, the starting point is Zulia, with possible expansion to Falcón as the agreed work develops.

In Guayana, the proposed work includes Bolívar and could extend to Delta Amacuro. It may examine power, industrial constraints, local authority, community positions and access. Each subject still needs a named asset, a clear question and a plan for obtaining the evidence.

sections.heading: Keep operating evidence and viability distinct
paragraphs: Evidence that an asset is active does not establish its contractual position. The proposed assessment considers contract standing, licence and sanctions standing, arbitration exposure, the counterparty’s ability to pay, operating access and security of tenure.

Each assessment needs a supporting document and a date. If the evidence is missing, leave the matter unassessed. A new event can require another review. It should not automatically determine a legal or contractual conclusion.

sections.heading: Match the output to what can safely be known
paragraphs: If a record can only be located to a state, show it at state level. A precise-looking facility pin would imply more knowledge than the evidence provides. Sensitive reporting can need further limits on what is disclosed, even when the location is known.

A regional brief should identify the client’s question, the changes relevant to it, the evidence that supports or disputes them and the next review. Partner and reporter identities, commercial terms and details that could expose a source should remain outside a public example.

watch: Which client decision sets the collection priority?
Is the location detail supported by evidence and safe to disclose?
Which assessments need a fresh review of their supporting documents?
